appraisal_events.evidence: Cela seul avait pour lui du prestige, infiniment plus de prestige que les Guermantes et tous les rois de la terre... elle a surtout un jugement merveilleux... elle a vraiment quelque chose de pythique.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator reports Robert's totalizing private admiration for his mistress, who eclipses in his eyes all aristocratic and social prestige, including the Guermantes and kings.

appraisal_events.evidence: il fallait la tenir par l'attente du lendemain... cet amour qu'elle avait pour lui n'empêchait pas qu'elle ne restât avec lui qu'à cause de son argent; C'est un peu cher pour moi en ce moment: trente mille francs.
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage exposes Robert's dependent, anxious position: he suspects she stays only for his money and must buy her continued attachment with an expensive gift, compromising his own leverage and judgment.

status_effects.explanation: In Robert's private evaluative world, she is elevated above every other source of worldly prestige.
Robert is shown as dependent on and practically subordinate to his mistress, needing to purchase her continued affection and doubting whether she loves him beyond his money.

ambiguities: Saint-Loup's mistress is never named in this passage (only 'son amie', 'sa maîtresse', 'elle'); she is identified as Rachel via the reference sheet rather than an in-passage proper name, so her presence is marked implicit and her canonical identity carries some uncertainty.

The narrator notes that Robert calls his mistress unremarkable-looking while clearly believing the opposite ('je vis bien qu'il pensait tout le contraire'), a small layer of irony about Robert's self-presentation that qualifies but does not reverse the dominant elevation in E1.
